# Installing software The Monday lab sessions are usually based on the material covered in the preceding Friday's lecture. In contrast, this lab session is focused on: * [installing the software](01.Software.html) that we will use during the module * Overview of the [anaconda navigator and jupyter-lab interface](02,Anaconda.html). In parallel with above, we want to review your existing data analysis skills: * Data analysis of the [Tips](03.Review_of_existing_skills.html) dataset __using software tools of your choice__. --- First, it might be a good idea to give a short primer on terminology: * __Programming Language__
Python is a __programming language__. It consists of a Python interpreter which can parse Python scripts (text files with .py extension) and execute them, and a collection of libraries/modules which extend the Python language adding capabilities such as game development, networking, database access, efficient data storage and processing, etc. * __Distributions__
One can install python directly from the [Python Software Foundation](http://www.python.org) but people have developed __distributions__ which also include commonly used python modules, editors and other tools useful when developing in python. [Anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com) is probably the most popular distribution for data mining. The full installation is large (about 6.39GB) but using it greatly simplifies setup and usage. * __Modules__
Like most programming languages, Python functionality can be increased by importing additional libraries or __modules__. When data mining the most popular modules are * pandas for data manipulation and input/output. * numpy for efficient processing of tablular data (used by pandas). * matplotlib for general 2D visualisation. * seaborn for statistical visualisations. * ... ... * __Package Manager__
Keeping track of the large number of modules in a python distribution is a non-trivial task due to incompatibilities between different versions of various modules — most of which have their own release schedules. A __package manager__ attempts to simplify this task. The default package manager in python is called pip, but within the Anaconda distribution the preferred package manager is conda. * __Editors/Interfaces__
You can perform all of your data mining activities using python scripts and an editor ([VSCode](https://code.visualstudio.com) is a excellent option), but an alternative interface has become standard in the data mining community which allows for more interactive development based on the concept of a notebook containing a mixture of code cells for execution and markdown cells for documentation.

jupyter-lab is (browser + local server based) interface for creating/editing/executing python notebooks.
Note, there is an alternate and older interface called jupyter-notebook. We would prefer that you do not use this. OK, enough background, let's start our first lab: * [Install a suitable Python environment](01.Software.html) * Overview of the [anaconda navigator and jupyter-lab interface](02.Anaconda.html). * [Review your existing data analysis skills using the Tips](03.Review_of_existing_skills.html) dataset __using software tools of your choice__.

los.title: Install / Verify a Suitable Python Environment
los.contentMd:
# Install / Verify a Suitable Python Environment **Contents** 1. [Background](#Background)
The tools that data science practitioners use have changed significantly in recent years. While we don't have time to go into much background detail here the next section mentions some of the main concepts and includes links for further reading. 2. [Installation](#Installation)
Next we cover installation of python using either a full [anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/products/individual) distribution (about 6.39 GB, based on options) or a reduced [miniconda](https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html) distribution (about 248MB). We would recommend you install the full anaconda distribution 2. [Extra Packages](#ExtraPackages)
In addition to the main python data analysis modules of [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org), [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/), etc., we will use numerous other modules which will be listed here. ## Background Traditionally, data mining was done using a suite of different tools: * Diagramming tools (such as MS Visio) for system specification. * ETL tools (such as [Pentaho Kettle, now part of Hitachi's DataOps suite](https://www.hitachivantara.com/en-us/products/data-management-analytics.html)) for acquiring data, often from operational databases and sometimes from data warehouses. * SQL scripts for combining and transforming the data en route (e.g., generating statistical summaries). * Proprietary statistical packages (such as [SAS](https://www.sas.com/en_us/software/enterprise-miner.html), [SPSS (now acquired by IBM)](https://www.ibm.com/us-en/marketplace/spss-modeler), etc.) for the more complex analyses and visualisations. * A mixture of languages and technologies (shell scripts, Java, C++, Javascript, etc.) to build the overall application that is deployed in production, e.g., to provide a web application for fraud checking. Nowadays we distinguish between two data mining usage patterns: * *exploring* the data and hence the underlying data-generating processes, and relating this data to a business/research objective, *by analysts*, * *adding value* by deploying the analysis procedures thus discovered to data in production, and integrating it with business processes, *by software engineers*. Traditional approaches introduce a lot of complexity (in the form of interfaces and context shifts) and require significant know-how, and are not optimal for either usage pattern. Many analysts like to use a single, GUI-based tool for their workflows. ISL `Clementine` (spun out from the University of Birmingham in the 1990s) was the tool that introduced the *workflow* metaphor and is now available as [IBM SPSS Modeler Professional](https://www.ibm.com/us-en/marketplace/spss-modeler). Such tools are expensive, which has encouraged competition from lower price/free equivalents. [KNIME](https://www.knime.org) is *one of* its (commercial) open source competitors (others include [RapidMiner](https://rapidminer.com/) and [orange](https://orange.biolab.si/)), using the same template as the original product but with enhanced features and performance. More recently, the [R](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-intro.pdf) (and [python](https://jakevdp.github.io/PythonDataScienceHandbook/)) data science communities have embraced the [literate programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literate_programming) paradigm of [Knitr](https://yihui.name/knitr) and [Jupyter](https://jupyter.org) *notebooks* which allows them to script function calls to powerful libraries, weaving this code with its own output (including graphs) and text that is typeset as LaTeX or markdown, respectively. Such code can be extracted and inserted into applications using Big Data frameworks with relatively little effort. Both the R and python data science communities are very active and solutions such as KNIME now position themselves as *platforms* that can be extended with user-provided modules written in a variety of languages, notably including R and python. Therefore, we will use [Jupyter (lab)](https://jupyter.org) as the primary learning tool/environment, both for sourcing the data and for the data mining process itself. ## Installation While any Python 3.13 distribution should be suitable for our needs, we recommend you either install a full [anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/products/individual) distribution (about 6.39 GB, based on options) or a reduced [miniconda](https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html) distribution (about 248MB). Which should you choose? To be honest, it doesn't really matter but if you want to: * get python development up and running quickly while suffering poor connection issues — use `miniconda`. * get more experience installing packages — use `miniconda`. * avoid (as much as possible) all that package management "stuff" — use `anaconda`. * play around and explore python tools — use `anaconda`. So a `miniconda` user will have faster initial download and less hard disk space used, but will need to install extra packages more frequently than an `anaconda` user. It is possible to have multiple python distributions installed on your system — you just have to manage the system paths so to allow you to switch between. Finally, there are other options — all of which should be suitable for this course's needs. However, while we are happy to help sort out issues our priority will be sorting issues in `anaconda` and `miniconda`. * Standard Python from [Python Software Foundation](https://www.python.org/). * On OS X using [homebrew](https://docs.brew.sh/Homebrew-and-Python) or [MacPorts](https://www.macports.org/), see [Thoughts on macOS Package Managers](https://saagarjha.com/blog/2019/04/26/thoughts-on-macos-package-managers/) which preferred MacPorts, nowadays homebrew is preferred (IMHO). * Homebrew with [pyenv](https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv) works nicely on OS X. * [uv](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) is the new cool tool that solves all installation problems. * [Enthought Deployment Manager (EDM)](https://assets.enthought.com/downloads/). ### Anaconda (Full python distribution) To install anaconda: * Pick any suitable 64-bit, Python 3.13 installer for you system from [anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/products/individual). * Run installer and default options should work for your system (But to be sure, read options and verify that any option like "Add python to PATH environment variable", "Increase length of PATH environment variable", or "Register Anaconda as my default Python" is enabled). Under MacOS, it is customary to install into the home directory, so will end up with a folder `~/anaconda3`. ### Miniconda (python distribution) To install miniconda: * Pick any suitable 64-bit, Python 3.13 installer for your system from [miniconda](https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html). * Run installer and default options should work for your system. Under OS X, a typical install will end up with a folder `~/miniconda3`. We will assume that people who select the miniconda know what they are doing and so the the rest of this guide is more focused on Anaconda not Miniconda. ### Verify Installation Regardless of anaconda/miniconda option you picked, once installed you should be able to run python from the command line. ~~~bash python ~~~ to get output and a python prompt similar to below (The important bit is "Python 3.11".) ~~~bash Python 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8 ] on darwin Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information. >>> ~~~ Type `1+1` at the prompt and press enter. You should get `2` or we are in trouble(!). ~~~python >>> 1+1 2 >>> quit() ~~~ Use `quit()` to exit the python shell and return to the command prompt. ## Extra Packages Both `anaconda` and `miniconda` use a package manager called `conda`. To install a package using anaconda, you can use the GUI or the command line as shown below. Miniconda does not offer the option of using a GUI. ~~~python conda install -y PACKAGE_NAME ~~~ The `-y` option causes the install to automatically carry out required installs/updated instead of asking for user confirmation. Note: some packages are not installable using `conda`, in these cases or if you are using a standard (non-anaconda variant) distribution you can install using the `pip` installer using ~~~python pip install PACKAGE_NAME ~~~ ### Side Note: Environments Both `conda` and `pip` support the idea of environments where within the one python distributions you might have a multiple of environments. This is to help avoid version conflicts between modules. `anaconda` and `miniconda` both start with one default environment called `base`. If you wish to use environments, you need to apply two steps: 1) create an environment using ~~~python conda create -n data_mining ~~~ and 2) activate it using ~~~bash conda activate data_mining ~~~ Since all of the packages that we plan to use work are (currently, Jan 2026) compatible, we won't need to use multiple environments, but they are a good idea and if you are interested there is a nice introduction at [ Happy Belly Bioinformatic](https://astrobiomike.github.io/unix/conda-intro). ### Packages that need installing if using `miniconda` ONLY ~~~python conda install -y numpy conda install -y scipy conda install -y matplotlib conda install -y seaborn conda install -c conda-forge -y jupyterlab ~~~ (we will update the above list during the semester, if needed) ### Packages that need installing if using `miniconda` or `anaconda` ~~~python conda install -c conda-forge -y dtale conda install -c conda-forge -y featuretools conda install -c anaconda -y graphviz conda install -c anaconda -y pydot conda install -c conda-forge -y phik conda install -c conda-forge -y pingouin ~~~ (We will update the above list during the semester, if needed.)

los.contentMd:
# Python tools This page is intended to be a minimal overview of the Anaconda distribution and jupyter-lab interface. For more detailed guides have a look at [Anaconda's official documentation](https://docs.anaconda.com/free/navigator/tutorials/index.html). ## Signup for AI Coding Help Recently added to the Anaconda Navigator is the ability to use AI to help with coding when using Jupyter-lab - this is our preferred IDE for this module. The use of AI in coding and in data mining is fundmentially changing the way we work, and it can both help and hinder our learning. We will talk more about this in the lectures, but we recommend that you do not use this AI coding feature within the jupyter-lab environment. Our goal here is to help you learn the material, and not just to produce the listed deliverables. ## Anaconda Navigator The Anaconda distribution supports a large number of python tools and to simplify their use, the distribution includes a small application called the _Anaconda Navigator_. For our purposes, there are two important items: * The _Environments_ tab, on the left, that opens graphical interface to the `conda` package manager. * The _jupyter-lab_ card near the top right, that starts the _jupyter-lab_ kernel back-end and opens the front-end in a browser window. On launching the jupyter-lab you should see the following Now click on `Python 3` notebook icon to get a new blank notebook: We will demo this interface in the pre-start lab, but for now our primary goal is that you have the software installed and working. ---

Today's Exercise

OK, that is enough setup for the moment.

Now we are going to put python aside for a moment and review your existing data analytics skills using a small dataset.

Review of existing skills

los.title: Data Exploration (Tips Dataset)
los.contentMd:
# Data Exploration (Tips Dataset) Using `python` with `pandas` and other modules does greatly simplify the data exploration process. However, we don't want you to get so focused on the tools that you overlook the actual process, and with enough masochism one could carry out all of the data exploration for this course using SQL, Excel, or even other programming languages. **So before we start on `python` and friends, we want you to explore a small dataset. You can use any software tool/environment that you like — our goal here is help you realise that (even if data science is new to you) that you might be bringing more skills to the table than you realise.** We start by downloading the dataset:
Download Tips dataset
Open this dataset using the software of your choice — excel, mysql, ... — and using your software examine the data. Typical things we look for include: * For each attribute (columns) find the following information. * The attribute type, e.g., nominal, ordinal, numeric. * Percentage of missing values in the data. * Statistical numerical measures — centre (mean, median, mode), spread (min, max, range, standard deviation), symmetry (skewness). * Statistical graphical representations — bar plots, histograms, ... even pie charts. * Are there any rows that have a value for the attribute that no other record has (i.e., unique values)? * Are there any outliers? * Which attributes seem to be linked? Later we will perform the same analysis using pandas, but for now the focus is on see what you can see when you look at data. When you are happy with exploring the data, try the following Moodle quiz.
Moodle Quiz
For those who are not registered on Moodle you will not be able to access the quiz. Instead you can download a [PDF with the questions](files/quiz_no_moodle.pdf) and attempt the quiz offline. Again, we hope to get all students on Moodle in a few days.

los.title: Tips
los.contentMd:
# Tips In our [Pre-Start Lab](../../01-Module_Overview/index.html#01-Pre-Start_Lab_-_Software_Setup) you looked at the [tips](files/data/tips.csv) dataset using whatever tools that you were familiar with. Today we will revisit the [tips](files/data/tips.csv) dataset using pandas while working within a jupyter-lab interface. ## Step 0 — Create suitable folder structure for data mining Create folder structure to keep your notebooks and dataset organised. Since we will use large datasets over multiple labs, we suggest you organise folders by dataset (not by practical/lab). So you could have folder tree like the following ~~~bash datasets/ ├── 01-Tips │   ├── 01-Tips_-_Import.ipynb │   ├── 02-Tips_-_EDA.ipynb │   └── data │   └── tips.csv ├── 02-Marks │   ├── 01-Top_X_Pandas_Commands.ipynb │   └── data │   └── marks.csv ├── 03-German_Credit │   ├── 01-German_Credit_-_Import.ipynb │   ├── 02-German_Credit_-_EDA.ipynb │   ├── 03-German_Credit_-_Model_Building.ipynb │   │── data │   │ └── german_credit.csv │   └── output ├── ... ~~~ The above file structure has a number of features that we find useful: * Structure is based around datasets — which often can be large, so we do not want to have multiple versions. * The number prefix (`01-` etc) is useful to ensure desired sort order in file viewer. * Within each dataset folder, the folder `data` contains the original dataset. For most of our datasets this will be just one or two files, but in general this could be arbitrary complicated. * We will use another folder, say `tmp` or `output` to store any intermediate data files that we generate during analysis. * The notebooks have naming convention: ``` PREFIX-DATASET_-_TASK.ipynb ``` where * `PREFIX` is a two-digit, zero-padded prefix to control sort order in file explorer and in jupyter-lab. * `DATASET` is the name of the dataset — this is useful when you have multiple notebooks open across multiple datasets. * `TASK` — the main data mining task that the notebook is focused on. ## Step 1 — Download and import dataset Download the dataset, [tips](files/data/tips.csv), and place it in your `data` folder. So following the above suggested structure, place it into folder `datasets/01-Tips/data`. ## Step 2 — Run up a `jupyter-lab` interface On Windows (assuming you have anaconda/miniconda) you:
  1. Start anaconda navigator and then Launch jupyter-lab
or (my preference, since I find the navigator to be slow)

  1. Go to the Windows start menu and select Anaconda Prompt under Anaconda3 (see image).
  2. At the prompt enter jupyter-lab
  3. Your browser should open showing interface similar to than shown below
On linux/OS X you:
  1. Open any terminal
  2. At the prompt enter jupyter-lab and a browser should open showing the jupyter-lab interface.
## Step 3 — Create new notebook and load in dataset. * Click on __Python 3__ Notebook. * By default the notebook name is `Untitled.ipynb`, for your own sanity you should rename this. I tend to follow convention

NUMBER-DATASET_-_TASK.ipynb

(where NUMBER, DATASET, and TASK are replaced by suitable short strings). * Import the core data science python packages ~~~python import numpy as np import pandas as pd pd.set_option('display.max_columns', None) import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns sns.set_style('darkgrid') ~~~ * Load the dataset to study. Notice the second and third line — they are there just to check that the dataset set was imported correctly. ~~~python df = pd.read_csv("data/tips.csv") print(df.shape) df.head() ~~~ ## Step 4 — Review Tips quiz Open the following quiz and start answering the questions, using markdown cells to add structure your notebook.
Data Analysis of Tips dataset (Using Pandas)
For any students who are not registered on Moodle you will not be able to access the quiz. Instead you can download a [PDF with the questions](files/Tips_quiz_no_moodle.pdf) and attempt the quiz offline. Again, we hope to get all students on Moodle by week 2. See figure below for my starting notebook. The slides [Top X Pandas Commands](../index.html#13-Top_X_pandas_commands) should be of use for pandas commands.

los.title: German Credit Dataset
los.contentMd:
# German Credit Dataset The German Credit dataset was used as part of the Statlog project, a European-based initiative in the 1990s to evaluate and compare a large number of machine learning algorithms on a range of different classification tasks. The dataset describes financial and banking details for customers and the task is to determine whether the customer is good or bad (column `Credit_Rating`). The task involves predicting whether a customer will pay back a loan. The dataset includes 1,000 observation and 20 input variables, 7 of which are numerical (integer) and 13 are categorical. In the target column `Credit_Rating`, there are two levels/classes: * Good Customers: Negative or majority class (70%). * Bad Customers: Positive or minority class (30%). ## Step 1 — Download and import dataset Download the dataset, [German Credit](files/data/german_credit.csv), and place it in your working folder. So following the above structure, place it into folder `datasets/03-German_Credit/data`. ## Step 2 — Create new notebook and load in dataset. * Change to folder `datasets/03-German_Credit`, and click on __Python 3__ Notebook. * By default the notebook name is `Untitled.ipynb`. I suggest you rename it to `01-German_Credit_-_Quiz.ipynb` or similar. * Import the core data science python packages ~~~python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns sns.set_style('darkgrid') ~~~ * Load the dataset to study. Notice the second and third line — they are there just to check that the dataset set was imported correctly. ~~~python df = pd.read_csv("data/german_credit.csv") print(df.shape) df.head() ~~~ ## Step 3 — Attempt quiz Open the following quiz and answer the questions, using markdown cells to add structure your notebook.
German Credit quiz
For those (currently 3 students) who are not registered on Moodle you will not be able to access the quiz. Instead you can download a [PDF with the questions](files/German_Credit_quiz_no_moodle.pdf) and attempt the quiz offline. Again, we hope to get all students on Moodle by week 2. Again the slides [Top X Pandas Commands](../index.html#06-Top_X_pandas_commands) should be of use.
